data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference unavoidably smuggles induction back in; any decision to act on a corroborated theory implicitly assumes the 'uniformity of nature' or that the future will resemble the past, rendering Popper's distinction between corroboration and probability practically null for the working scientist.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a non-inductive basis for practical action can be demonstrated (e.g., purely evolutionary selection of habits).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper admits that his philosophy offers no guide for action, only for criticism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Decision-theoretic inevitability: To choose Theory A over Theory B for action implies an expectation that A will yield better outcomes. This expectation can only be derived from A's past performance if one assumes the future resembles the past (the principle of induction).
